author: Euan Sinclair
title: Core thesis: variance premium is the primary edge
body: Implied volatility is almost always overpriced relative to subsequent realized volatility. This variance premium is the most robust empirical fact in options markets. The correct approach is to find robust edge backed by empirical evidence, choose the option structure to monetize it, size appropriately, and always remember how much you don't know. Variance premium is persistent (a risk premium), not an inefficiency that will erode.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: BSM as parameterization tool, not pricing model
body: The market prices options through supply and demand. BSM converts market prices into a single comparable parameter — implied volatility. This is why traders speak in IV terms: BSM lets you compare options across strikes, expirations, and underlyings on a common scale. If BSM were perfect, a single constant IV would describe all options on the same underlying. The volatility smile/skew is simply evidence that BSM is an imperfect model — not a market failure.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Delta-hedged P/L formula: the foundation of vol trading
body: For a delta-hedged option position held over a small interval dt, the P/L is: Profit = ½Γ·S²·(σ_realized² − σ_implied²)·dt. This means: if realized vol exceeds implied vol, you profit; if it falls short, you lose. Magnitude depends on gamma (highest ATM) and the squared difference between realized and implied vol. This is the core equation of volatility trading — everything else follows from it.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: BSM: drift is irrelevant for market makers who hedge
body: Market makers who continuously buy/sell the underlying to replicate an option can guarantee a profit regardless of where the underlying goes. Because the replication cost doesn't depend on drift, drift doesn't appear in BSM. This is correct for hedgers. But it is wrong for speculators who buy options to benefit from directional moves — for them drift matters, and BSM systematically misprices options relative to their speculative value.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: BSM assumptions all violated in practice
body: BSM assumes: constant volatility, continuous trading, no transaction costs, normally distributed returns, single risk-free rate, unlimited short selling. All are violated. The volatility smile shows non-constant vol; fat tails show non-normality; transaction costs are real; trading is discrete. Despite this, BSM remains useful as a shared measurement standard because everyone uses it to convert prices to IV — its value is as a common language, not as truth.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: SPY implied volatility surface: 3D structure across strikes and time
body: Figure 1.1: SPY IV surface on September 10, 2019 (3D plot). X-axis: Strike 200–330. Y-axis: Time to expiry 31–122 days. Z-axis: IV 0–40%. The surface slopes upward for lower strikes (volatility skew: OTM puts have higher IV than ATM). The term structure is generally flat or slightly humped. The 3D surface shows the full BSM parameterization of the options market — every combination of strike and expiry has its own IV, confirming BSM is not a constant-vol model but a flexible parameterization framework.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Hedging frequency tradeoff: variance vs transaction costs
body: Figure 1.4: Straddle P/L standard deviation vs number of hedges (0–250 per year). SD declines from ~$650 at zero hedges to ~$300 at 250 hedges — a convex declining curve. The first 20–30 hedges per year eliminate most directional variance; beyond 50 hedges adds little further reduction but increases transaction costs. Figures 1.2–1.3: Unhedged short straddle has strongly right-skewed P/L distribution (fat left tail). Daily-hedged straddle has near-normal, symmetric distribution. Practical implication: most retail/positional traders should hedge infrequently, accepting wider P/L variance in exchange for avoiding transaction cost drag.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Discipline without edge is faster failure
body: A trader without a real edge who applies strict discipline will lose money faster and more consistently than a sloppy trader with the same bad strategy. The first task in trading is identifying genuine edge — not managing a strategy without it. Risk management can only scale an edge up or down; it cannot create edge from nothing. Optimism and overconfidence are as dangerous as lack of discipline.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Risk premium vs behavioral inefficiency: critical distinction
body: Risk premia are structural payments from parties seeking insurance. The variance premium is the premier example: investors buy options for portfolio protection and rationally pay above fair value, just as homeowners overpay for fire insurance. Risk premia persist because structural demand for insurance persists. Behavioral inefficiencies are temporary mispricings from cognitive biases. These erode once discovered and widely traded. Post-earnings drift is an example. Distinguishing the two matters: strategies built on risk premia have structural persistence; strategies built on inefficiencies have a finite exploitation window.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: White Reality Check: testing for data mining bias
body: The White Reality Check and Hansen's SPA test detect whether apparent outperformance in backtests results from overfitting to historical data. Without such tests, most 'edges' discovered through large-scale parameter search are artifacts. Requirements for a genuine edge: (1) strong statistical evidence across multiple markets and time periods, (2) a specific, predictive mechanism — not just 'behavioral bias,' (3) survival after controlling for known risk factors, (4) is it a risk premium (persistent) or inefficiency (temporary)?

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Volatility forecasting is implicit in every option trade
body: Every option trade is an implicit volatility forecast. Even the choice to sell options 'because vol is high' is a forecast that realized vol will be lower than implied. The relevant question is not whether to forecast but how. Methods: historical rolling vol (simple but suffers from ghost effects), EWMA (weights recent data more heavily, adapts faster), GARCH(1,1) (captures vol clustering and mean reversion), VIX (market-implied, best for SPX). Empirical finding: all methods perform similarly — differences of ~0.5 vol points in average error. Model selection matters less than having a systematic process.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: EWMA volatility model: formula and rolling vol chart
body: Figure 3.1: Maximus Inc. 30-day rolling vol shows clustering and mean reversion — the motivation for EWMA. Equation 3.2: σ²_t = λ·σ²_{t-1} + (1−λ)·r²_{t-1}. λ (decay factor) typically 0.9–0.95. λ=0.94 is the RiskMetrics standard. EWMA weights recent returns more heavily than older ones, adapting faster to regime changes than equal-weighted rolling windows. Avoids the 'ghost effect' where a large return suddenly drops out of the lookback window and causes an artificial vol spike.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: GARCH(1,1): captures vol clustering and mean reversion
body: GARCH(1,1): σ²_t = ω + α·r²_{t-1} + β·σ²_{t-1}. α captures vol clustering (high vol follows high vol — today's large return increases tomorrow's vol). β captures persistence (yesterday's vol forecast influences today). ω/(1−α−β) = long-run unconditional variance. Figure 3.2: GARCH term structure of forecast vol for SPY — both GARCH(1,1) (solid) and GJR-GARCH (dashed) start at ~20% and decay to ~10% over 120 days. At long horizons, reversion to the long-run mean dominates — forecasting mean reversion is the primary contribution of GARCH for long-horizon estimates.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: VIX as predictor and VIX term structure contango
body: VIX has predictive advantage for SPX volatility over statistical models because it incorporates market information. VIX futures are normally in contango (longer-dated > spot). Cash VIX is a better predictor of future VIX than the futures price. The term structure is in contango 81% of the time (2006 to start of 2019). When in contango, VIX futures converge downward toward spot as expiration approaches, creating persistent roll yield for short VIX positions. Selling front-month VIX futures when term structure is steep captures both roll yield and variance premium.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: VIX short strategy: P/L charts and contango filter
body: Figure 4.1–4.3: Selling front-month VIX futures from June 2015 to October 2019. Unfiltered: cumulative P/L rises to ~$80,000 with a sharp ~$30,000 drawdown in February 2018 (XIV collapse). VIX chart (Fig 4.2) shows baseline of 10–20 then spike to ~37 in Feb 2018. Contango-filtered (Fig 4.3): similar overall profit but smoother equity curve — the filter reduces exposure during dangerous regimes. Confirms VIX term structure contango is a useful timing filter, not just a theoretical construct.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Variance premium SPX: statistics, distribution, and time series
body: Figure 4.4: VIX vs S&P 500 30-day realized vol (1990–2018). VIX (orange) almost always runs above realized vol (blue) — both spiked to 80–90% in 2008. Figure 4.5: Variance premium time series (VIX − realized vol). Almost always positive, with large negative spikes only at major crises (1997, 1998, 2001, 2008, 2011, 2018). Figure 4.6: Premium distribution histogram. Table 4.1 Summary Stats: Mean=4.08, SD=5.96, Skewness=−2.33, Max=31.21, Min=−53.3, Median=4.63, 90th Pct=9.62, 10th Pct=−1.45. The premium is persistently positive with catastrophic left tail events. Average 4 vol points above realized vol — the systematic short-vol edge.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: CNDR and BFLY indexes: 30 years of variance premium capture
body: Figure 4.7: CBOE CNDR (Condor) Index 1988–2018 — sells monthly SPX iron condors. Cumulative value: 100 → ~1,200 over 30 years. Figure 4.8: CBOE BFLY (Butterfly) Index 1988–2018 — similar strategy, more volatile, cumulative 100 → ~800. Both show that systematic short-vol structures on SPX have delivered strong long-run performance across three decades including major crises (2001, 2008). However, both strategies experienced severe drawdowns during crises — confirming the risk premium nature of the variance premium (you earn it by bearing crash risk).

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Cross-asset variance premia: commodities and correlations
body: Table 4.4 — Commodity variance premia: Oats 6.2%, Lumber 3.5%, Cocoa 3%, Rice 3%, OJ 2.3%, Copper 2.4%, Coffee 1.7%, Gold 1%, Silver 0.2%. Table 4.5 — Within-sector correlation of VP: Energy 33.4%, Grains 24.2%, Livestock 31.4%, Metals 30.1%. Table 4.6 — Cross-sector correlation: Energy-S&P 26.5%, Grains-S&P 2%, Metals-S&P 30.7%, T-bonds-S&P 39.3%. Commodities are largely uncorrelated to equity variance premium, making them excellent diversifiers in a short-vol portfolio. T-bonds do NOT hedge equity short-vol risk (positive 39% correlation).

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Why the variance premium exists and will persist
body: Three structural reasons the variance premium will persist: (1) Insurance demand: investors with long portfolios buy puts for downside protection, paying above fair value just as homeowners overpay for fire insurance. Structural demand. (2) Path-dependency (Figs 4.9–4.10): investors care about the path to terminal wealth, not just the terminal value. They pay extra for options that prevent painful intra-period drawdowns. This is rational, not a bias. (3) Uncertainty premium: options insure against model failure — the possibility that vol will be much higher than anyone estimates. In a world with parameter uncertainty, this is rational.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Peso problem: short vol P/L looks smooth until it isn't
body: Figures 4.11–4.12: A short put's P/L stays flat at ~$1.50–$2.50 for 20 days collecting theta, then spikes to $3.50 when a favorable stock jump occurs on day 21. A long call mirrors this: bleeds slightly negative for 20 days, then spikes to +$3 on jump. The 'Peso Problem': strategies can appear deceptively smooth because catastrophic events (extreme moves, crashes) are rare enough to not appear in any given sample. Historical data with no large crashes overstates the true edge of short-vol strategies. Always size for the event you haven't seen yet.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Variance premium: high VIX = highest premium BUT highest risk
body: The variance premium is NOT always present. In crash events, realized vol massively exceeds implied vol. The premium is largest when VIX is high — precisely when the risk of further vol escalation is also highest. VIX quintile assessment: VIX < 13: Poor risk/reward (premium small, gamma high); VIX 13–20: Best environment (moderate premium, manageable risk); VIX 20–25: Acceptable with sizing; VIX > 25: Reduce size significantly. Do NOT sell volatility after a spike without reducing size. Crowding risk: as more capital chases the premium, it may compress and gap-down risk concentrates.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: 11 tradeable effects: confidence level 3 (highest)
body: Level 3 (highest confidence): (1) Variance premium — sell IV broadly on indices and stocks where IV > realized vol. (2) Earnings IV overpricing — IV of options expiring shortly after earnings overstates the subsequent move by ~30% on average. Sell straddles/strangles before earnings. (3) VIX term structure contango — sell front-month VIX futures when term structure is steep. These effects have: strong statistical evidence across multiple periods and markets, specific predictive mechanisms, and persistent structural causes.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Earnings straddle: long before, short at announcement
body: Figure 5.1 (long straddle): Buying ATM straddles 10 days before earnings for 73 large-cap stocks (2005–2010). 43% of trades profitable, win/loss ratio 1.70. Cumulative P/L rose steadily to ~$40,000 over 24 earnings periods on $10,000 notional. Figure 5.2 (short straddle): Selling ATM straddles as close as possible to earnings. 64% profitable, win/loss ratio 0.69. Skewness −5.4, excess kurtosis 12.2 — high win rate but occasional large losses. Key insight: earnings vol is overpriced on average (30% overstatement), but both strategies carry significant tail risk from occasional huge moves.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) and earnings reversals
body: PEAD (Confidence Level 2): stocks continue moving in the direction of the earnings surprise for 60+ days. Strongest for small caps. Trade: buy calls/puts in direction of the surprise after announcement. Win/loss ratio 1.70, but must verify each case. Earnings reversals (Confidence Level 2): some stocks overshoot on earnings day and partially reverse over the next week. Fade very large moves (>10% on high volume). FOMC vol (Confidence Level 2): implied vol around FOMC announcements overstates subsequent moves. Short straddles into FOMC dates have historically positive expected value.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Short straddle P/L distributions: fair vs mispriced
body: Figure 6.1 (fairly priced): Short straddle P/L — large spike at max profit ($841), long left tail. Average $8, SD $1,882, Skewness −1.83, Kurtosis 6.41, Median $384, 10th Pct −$2,274, Min −$15,321, Profitable 57%. Figure 6.3 (mispriced, realized vol=70%): distribution shifts left, wider, clearly negative EV. Table 6.3 (mispriced straddle): Average −$3,071, SD $5,425, Skew −4.31, Kurtosis 29.01, Min −$94,084, Profitable 25%. Core lesson: the short straddle has positive EV ONLY when you are right about the variance premium. Negative skew and high kurtosis are always present — manage size accordingly.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Short strangle distributions vs straddle: higher win rate, worse tails
body: Figure 6.2 (fairly priced strangle): extremely sharp spike at max profit ($841), even higher win rate than straddle. Table 6.2: Average −$6.12, SD $2,140, Skew −4.8, Kurtosis 24.2, Median $841, 10th Pct −$1,994, Min −$27,683, Profitable 78%. Table 6.4 (mispriced strangle): Average −$3,230, SD $9,190, Skew −4.2, Min −$197,526, Profitable 36%. Strangles hit max profit 78% of the time vs 57% for straddles, but when they lose, they lose much more (min −$197K vs −$15K). The strangle appears safer but has dramatically worse tail risk.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Delta-hedged straddle vs strangle: taming the distribution
body: Figures 6.7–6.8: Delta-hedging daily dramatically narrows the P/L distribution. Hedged straddle range: roughly −$5,000 to +$1,000 (vs −$15,000 unhedged). Table 6.8 — Hedged Straddle vs Strangle: Straddle: Avg $7, Median $12, Skew −0.2, Kurtosis 1.28, Worst −$856, Worst Decile −$242. Strangle: Avg $22, Median $126, Skew −2.71, Kurtosis 13.32, Worst −$2,170, Worst Decile −$450. Figure 6.9: Vega profile — straddle has narrow ATM peak; strangle has wider bimodal profile. Key: after delta-hedging, the straddle has better tail properties than the strangle, but the strangle retains higher average return. Trader preference depends on skew tolerance.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Butterfly and condor P/L distributions: capped risk structures
body: Figures 6.10–6.13: Fairly priced butterfly: bimodal — spike at max profit ($2,756) when stock stays between wings, and spike at partial loss near strikes. Table 6.9: Avg −$25, SD $2,460, Skew 0.4, profitable 46%. Fairly priced condor: Table 6.10: Avg −$9, SD $2,252, Skew −0.4, profitable 58%. Badly priced structures (Tables 6.11–6.12): results flip dramatically — badly priced butterfly: profitable only 20%, mostly at max loss. Condor: profitable 26%. Conclusion: butterflies and condors only work when the short strikes are genuinely overpriced. They limit max loss but offer no edge if the vol premium isn't there.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Straddle spread vs short straddle: risk reduction with similar return
body: Table 6.15 — Short Straddle vs Straddle Spread (short front-month, long back-month): Straddle: Avg $261, SD $597, Skew −1.4, Max $899, Min −$3,753, Profitable 72%. Spread: Avg $265, SD $210, Skew 0.0, Max $578, Min −$66, Profitable 87%. Figure 6.14: Straddle spread P/L at expiry — tent shape peaking at ~$6 ATM, flat at edges. The spread reduces worst-case loss by 50× (from −$3,753 to −$66) and increases win rate (87% vs 72%) with essentially the same average return. Cost: slightly capped upside. Best use: when vol is elevated and you want downside protection.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Implied vol skew: OTM puts systematically overpriced
body: Table 6.18 — SPY put implied vols on July 30, 2019. IV declines monotonically from deep OTM puts (strike 210, IV=0.253) to near ATM (strike 290, IV=0.160). This skew is persistent — far-OTM puts carry a much larger volatility premium than ATM options. The skew reflects: crash risk demand (investors pay for downside insurance), risk-neutral measure overweighting crashes vs physical measure, and systemic leverage. Selling OTM puts collects BOTH the variance premium AND the skew premium. Rule of thumb: SPX 10-delta put IV ≈ 1.45× ATM IV; 25-delta call IV ≈ 0.88× ATM IV.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Hedging short OTM puts: choosing the right spread
body: Table 6.22: For a short 260 put position, hedging with different long put strikes. Strike 180 costs $0.64 but limits max loss to $7,436. Strike 220 costs $2.25, limits to $3,597. ATM option price approximation (Eq 6.2): P ≈ 0.4Sσ√T. This formula gives a quick estimate of option fair value for mental calculations. Key principle: higher-strike hedges cost more but provide better protection. The skew means OTM puts get progressively more expensive per unit of protection, favoring using a single option closer to ATM rather than multiple cheaper far-OTM options.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Strike selection: precision of forecast determines optimal structure
body: Table 7.1: Options on a $100 stock. If stock goes to $120: 95-strike → $187 profit, 100-strike → $257, 105-strike → $369, 110-strike → $567. But if stock only goes to $106: 95-strike → $26, 100-strike → $7, 105-strike → −$68, 110-strike → −$100. A correct directional call on the wrong strike can produce a loss. The higher the confidence in the magnitude of the move, the more aggressive the strike selection. Uncertainty about magnitude favors ATM strikes; high-conviction big moves favor OTM strikes.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Boness model: subjective option pricing with drift
body: BSM is correct for market makers who hedge. For speculators with directional views, the Boness model (1962) uses the trader's actual drift forecast μ: Call: C = S·exp(μT)·N(d₃) − X·N(d₄) where d₃ = [ln(S/X) + (μ + σ²/2)·T] / (σ√T) and d₄ = [ln(S/X) + (μ − σ²/2)·T] / (σ√T). If Boness value > market price, the option is underpriced relative to your forecast. Even a modest directional forecast (μ = 3% above risk-free) meaningfully changes option value. Partial derivative ∂C/∂μ = T·S·exp(μT)·N(d₃) — larger for longer-dated options.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: True ITM probability N(d₄) vs risk-neutral N(d₂)
body: BSM's N(d₂) is the risk-neutral probability (correct for hedging and replication). The true physical-measure probability of expiring ITM is N(d₄) from the Boness model. Example: 1-year 110-call, S=$100, σ=30%, r=0%, μ=10%: N(d₂) = 32% (risk-neutral), N(d₄) = 45% (physical). Difference = 13 percentage points. For a speculative buyer with a 10% drift forecast, the option has a 45% chance of paying off, not 32%. Using N(d₂) = 32% to evaluate 'is this worth buying?' gives the wrong answer. Speculators should always evaluate options using N(d₄) with their own drift forecast.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Option return moments: inherent positive skew of long options
body: Long call options have positively skewed return distributions independent of any directional forecast: maximum loss is limited to premium paid, while upside is theoretically unlimited. Most expire worthless (frequent small losses) but occasional large winners. This positive skewness makes long options attractive even at BSM fair value for speculators who prefer positive-skew instruments. Short options have the opposite skewness — frequent small wins but potential for large losses.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Long stock vs long call vs call spread: P/L distributions compared
body: For $100 stock, μ=20%, σ=30%, zero rates: Long stock (Fig 8.1, Table 8.1): Avg $2,640, SD $3,736, Skew 1.12, Profitable 75%. Long ATM call (Fig 8.2, Table 8.2): Avg $1,516, SD $3,198, Skew 1.66, Profitable (lower). ATM/20-delta call spread (Fig 8.3, Table 8.3): Avg $819, SD $1,502, Skew 0.01, Profitable 58%. Lower average for call spread but much lower SD — the spread caps both win and loss. Long call has higher skew (more lottery-like) than stock at lower average return. Structure selection depends on: size of directional forecast confidence, skew preference, and whether variance premium is present (if IV < expected realized, long calls have extra edge).

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Short put vs covered call: P/L distribution comparison
body: Short ATM put (Fig 8.4, Table 8.4): Avg $706, SD $986, Skew −2.22, Kurtosis 4.53, Median $1,192, Profitable 78%. Heavily right-skewed — spike at max profit. Covered call payoff (Fig 8.5): hockey-stick shape with upside capped at strike + premium. Key insight: short put is synthetically equivalent to covered call (put-call parity). Both collect the variance premium while capping upside. Short put is simpler to execute and has similar risk/reward. Choose based on transaction costs, margin, and directional conviction.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Covered call (BXM index): superior risk-adjusted returns to buy-and-hold
body: Figure 8.6: BXM (CBOE covered call on SPX) vs S&P 500 from 1988–2019. Table 8.5: BXM Annual Return 8.5%, Vol 12.6%, Max Drawdown 40.1%, Skew −0.67. S&P 500: Annual 7.7%, Vol 17.3%, Max Drawdown 56.8%, Skew −0.29. BXM achieves higher return with 27% lower vol and 29% smaller max drawdown. Table 8.6: BXMD (30-delta calls) even better: Annual 10.3%, Vol 14.7%. Figure 8.7 shows vol premium peaks near ATM — selling ATM covered calls maximizes variance premium capture while selling farther OTM gives more delta exposure but less vol premium.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Short put spread and risk reversal: directional + vol premium trades
body: Short ATM/20-delta put spread (Fig 8.8, Tables 8.7–8.8): With flat vol: Avg $422, SD $680, Skew −1.42, Profitable 78%. With vol skew (OTM put at 40.8% IV): Avg $216, lower but still positive EV. Risk reversal (short 20-delta put, long 20-delta call, Fig 8.9, Table 8.9): Avg $948, SD $2,140, Skew 2.69, Kurtosis 9.00, Profitable 85%. Risk reversal profits greatly from upside moves and is long positive skew — best when bullish AND skew premium is steep (OTM put overpriced vs call). One-by-two call spread (Fig 8.10): bimodal distribution, riskier — use only with very high directional conviction.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Variance and skew premia dominate over directional accuracy
body: General principle: variance and skew premia are more important to position profitability than getting the directional call right. A moderately wrong directional view with a short-vol structure can still be profitable if the vol premium is captured. Crash hedge comparison (Tables 8.13–8.14): one-by-two put spread provides better downside protection (higher P/L at −30% and −20% moves) than single OTM put, because the ratio structure collects skew premium from the overpriced short-strike put leg. The skew makes ratio spreads structurally attractive for crash hedges.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Kelly criterion: optimal bet fraction for continuous returns
body: For a strategy with mean return μ and standard deviation σ: f* ≈ μ/σ² (equivalent to Sharpe ratio × σ). For non-normal returns (negative skew, as in short-vol): f* ≈ μ/(μ²+σ²) + λ₃·μ²/(μ²+σ²)³ where λ₃ is the third central moment. Negative skewness (typical for short-vol strategies) reduces optimal Kelly fraction below the naive symmetric estimate. Figure 9.1: Kelly growth rate as function of f — bell-shaped curve, peaks at small fraction (~0.06) when a −3× outcome has 2% probability. Rare catastrophic events drastically reduce the optimal Kelly fraction.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Kelly with tail events: rare disasters dominate optimal fraction
body: Figure 9.2: Adding a rare tail event (P3=1%, W3=−3×) to a three-outcome model. Growth rate curve peaks at much lower f (~0.03) vs the base case, and turns sharply negative at f>0.10. Equation 9.3: B_n = B_{n-1} + f·B_{n-1}·g(X_n). Key insight: a 1% probability of losing 3× stake reduces the optimal Kelly fraction to very small values. This is the mathematical reason why short-vol strategies require much smaller position sizes than naive Kelly estimates suggest — the fat-tail events that appear rarely in historical data may dominate the optimal fraction.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Kelly estimation uncertainty: full Kelly almost always means over-betting
body: The Kelly fraction is estimated from historical data with finite sample size. With n=1,000 trades: sd(f̂) ≈ 0.03–0.10 depending on strategy. There is a meaningful probability that estimated f* > 0 while the true f* ≤ 0. Equations 9.26–9.32: Variance of Kelly estimate via delta method: Var(f̂) = (1/σ² + 2μ²/σ⁴)/n. Equations 9.33–9.37: With skewness correction: sd(f̂) = √(1/σ² + 2μ²/σ⁴)/(n−1). Fractional Kelly tables: to keep over-betting probability below 10% with skew adjustment, scale Kelly by 0.205×; below 20%: scale by 0.478×. Practical default: trade at 25–50% of estimated Kelly.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Kelly growth rate formula and half-Kelly as risk-efficiency optimum
body: Growth rate: GR(f) = (f − f²/2)·μ²/σ². Table 9.2: Scale factors to keep over-betting probability below target levels. Equation 9.38: Prob(f < f*) = Z((f − f*)·√(n−1) / sd(f̂)). Figure 9.5: Fractional Kelly scaling factors by confidence level. GR is maximized at f=1 (full Kelly), falls to zero at f=2, negative for f>2. The growth-rate-to-drawdown ratio peaks at f=0.5 (half-Kelly). Half-Kelly maximizes risk-adjusted returns — gives the most growth per unit of drawdown. Equations 9.39–9.40: Ruin probability P(A,B) = (1−A^(1−2/f))/(B^(1−2/f)−A^(1−2/f)).

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Kelly ruin probability: more aggressive betting does NOT improve survival
body: Figures 9.6–9.7: Growth rate and growth-rate-to-drawdown ratio as functions of Kelly fraction. Growth peaks at full Kelly; growth-to-drawdown ratio peaks at half-Kelly. Equation 9.40: Ruin probability formula — probability of doubling before ruin. Counterintuitively: at very low f (0.1× Kelly), ruin probability ~90% before doubling. At full Kelly: ruin probability ~45%. At 2× Kelly: worse than full Kelly. Figure 9.8: Ruin probability curve. Figure 9.9: Expected time to reach target. Equation 9.41: E[T] = expected time to reach goal. Trading at 25–50% Kelly gives best combination of growth efficiency AND survival probability.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Stops fundamentally change return distribution shape
body: Figures 9.10–9.13 show what stops actually do: Figure 9.10: Strategy return distribution — normal, mean 10%, SD 15%. Figure 9.11 (hoped-for): Naive view — stop just truncates left tail at −15%. This is wrong. Figure 9.12 (true fixed stop): Bimodal distribution — mass of stopped trades collapses to a point at −15%, PLUS surviving trades have modified distribution. Average drops to 9.6%. Figure 9.13 (trailing stop): Right tail severely truncated — max return ~20%. Mean drops to 9.4%. Stops eliminate recovering winners, not just large losers. Use stops only when position monitoring is impossible or the drawdown risk is genuinely existential.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Subaccount method: quarter-Kelly vs fixed stop comparison
body: Figure 9.14: Quarter-Kelly final account distribution — bell-shaped, range $78–$130. Figure 9.15: Equivalent subaccount method (full Kelly on $43.70 subaccount) — same distribution. Figure 9.16: 43.7% subaccount — broader distribution. Table 9.4 — Quarter Kelly vs Fixed Stop vs Trailing Stop: Quarter-Kelly: Avg $101.70, Min $78.30, Avg DD 9%, Max DD 26%. Fixed Stop: Avg $102.20, Min $68.75, Avg DD 12%, Max DD 38%. Trailing: Avg $117.13, Min $69.36, Avg DD 12%, Max DD 30%. Quarter-Kelly has smallest drawdowns of all three. Trailing stop has highest average return but also highest volatility and a long-shot of extreme gains/losses.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Bitcoin: extreme vol and counterparty risks dwarf any variance premium
body: Figure 10.1: Bitcoin price USD 2018 — peaked near $17,700 in January, fell to $3,000 by year-end. Annualized vol ~68% vs SPX ~15%, EUR/USD ~7%. The variance premium likely exists in crypto options, but counterparty risks are extreme: QuadrigaCX (CEO dies with all passwords, customers lose $190M), exchange hacks, no regulatory oversight. Average currency vol is in single digits; crypto is 10× more volatile. Crypto options cannot be directly compared to regulated market options. Any edge from variance premium is more than offset by counterparty and regulatory risk.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Meta risks: counterparty failure kills portfolios independent of strategy
body: Market risk is well-understood. Meta risks — counterparty failure, fraud, regulatory changes, liquidity crises — are underappreciated and can cause total loss regardless of strategy quality. Historical examples: MF Global (2011, customer funds misused), Madoff (Ponzi scheme), QuadrigaCX (crypto exchange, CEO holds all keys), Sumitomo copper (price manipulation). Risk mitigation: multiple brokers, prefer regulated exchanges, maintain excess capital outside trading accounts, never concentrate with single counterparty, verify track records with audited returns. Never invest in strategies you don't understand.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Interest rate and dividend adjustments to BSM
body: Interest rates: daily rate changes have SD of 0.037% vs VIX daily changes of 1.7 points. Rate uncertainty is negligible relative to vol uncertainty — stochastic rate models add no practical value for option traders. Dividends: adjust S → S − PV(dividends). American calls: early exercise optimal just before ex-dividend date when dividend > remaining time value. The magnitude of required rate corrections vs vol corrections is typically 10:1 in favor of vol corrections — vol forecasting is far more important than rate modeling.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Imperfect hedge correlation: Figure A1.3 shows residual risk
body: Figure A1.3: SD of P/L for an option hedged with imperfectly correlated underlying. X-axis: Correlation 0–1. Y-axis: SD($) 0–$40,000. At correlation=0: SD ~$35,000 (essentially unhedged). At correlation=0.9: SD ~$10,000 (still substantial residual risk). At correlation=1.0: SD=0 (perfect hedge). Practical implication: using SPY to hedge an individual stock with 70–80% correlation leaves ~25% of the P/L variance unhedged. Proxy hedging is much better than no hedging but not close to perfect hedging.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Mixture-of-normals model: explaining fat tails and volatility regimes
body: Figure A1.4 and Equation A1.4: S&P 500 returns modeled as mixture of two normal distributions: low-vol regime (~10–15% annualized) and high-vol regime (~30–80% annualized). Kurtosis formula: 3·(p₁σ₁²+p₂σ₂²)²/(p₁σ₁²+p₂σ₂²)². This two-regime mixture explains the observed leptokurtosis of equity returns without assuming non-normal distributions within regimes. The S&P switches between regimes — normal markets at 10–15% vol, crisis markets at 30–80%. Implication: the fat tails in equity option prices are rational pricing for regime switches, not irrational fear.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Rule of Five and Rule of Three: quick statistical heuristics
body: Rule of Five: if 5 observations all lie above a threshold, 93.75% confidence the population median is above that threshold (probability = 1 − 2×(0.5)⁵ = 0.9375). Rule of Three (Equation A2.3): upper 95% bound on probability of a rare event = 3/n, where n is the number of observations without seeing the event. Derivation (Eq A2.4): (1−p)^n = 0.05 → p = 1−0.05^(1/n) ≈ 3/n for large n. Example: never lost >15% in 100 trades → 95% upper bound on that loss probability = 3/100 = 3%. These quick heuristics allow traders to make statistical inferences without full distribution fitting.

author: Euan Sinclair
title: Effective bid-ask spread: far wider than posted for large orders
body: Table A3.1: UVXY order book (August 10, 2016). Best bid 20.64, best ask 20.65 — posted spread $0.01. But buying 5,000 shares requires walking up the book to 20.69, giving an effective spread of $0.0612 — 6× the posted spread. Key principle: value trades against the decision price (mid-price), not the bid or ask. This prevents being psychologically intimidated into worse fills. For options: the indicated spread might be bid 9.0 for 100 options, but the actual effective spread for larger sizes is always wider. Always estimate true execution cost before trading, especially for large positions in less liquid instruments.
